newsitem.title: USA: Florida to seek stay of decision prisoner release.
newsitem.headline: Florida to seek stay of decision prisoner release.

text.p: Florida will ask a state appellate court to postpone the release of thousands of violent prison inmates until the U.S. Supreme Court rules on the issue, officials said Friday.

The request, expected to be filed early next week, follows a ruling by the Florida Supreme Court that threw out an administrative rule now being used by the state to keep more than 20,000 violent criminals behind bars.

State officials said a case being considered by the U.S. high court could answer the question once and for all: Can a rule adopted by the Florida Department of Corrections this year requiring violent prisoners to serve 85 percent of their sentences apply to inmates sentenced before it took effect?

"We're asking the appellate court to re-hear and stay this case pending the outcome of a U.S. Supreme Court case that covers virtually the same issues," Florida Deputy Attorney General Peter Antonacci said.

"We don't want Florida to have one interpretation and the rest of the world will have another," he said. "We're hoping the appellate court will stay the (state supreme court) decision pending the outcome in Washington."

Nearly 1,500 inmates of state prisons could be eligible for parole after the state supreme court struck down the rule. Overcrowding in Florida's prisons in the 1980s had prompted officials to adopt generous early release provisions, with some inmates earning up to three weeks for every month served.

Florida's Attorney General ruled this year that corrections officials could use their discretion to prohibit early release for certain classes of violent criminals, and in April correction officials adopted a rule prohibiting release for inmates sentenced for murder, sex crimes, assault and a host of other violent offenses.

The department extended those rules to about 20,000 inmates, some of whom were sentenced up to 20 years ago. In a unanimous decision, the Florida Supreme Court ruled that inmates sentenced before the rule change could not be held to the more stringent standards.
